claims.text: Molecular dynamics simulations can be used to study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles as a function of size.
The thermal stability of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles is size-dependent.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles melt or become disordered at lower temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher surface-to-volume ratio than larger nanoparticles.
A higher surface-to-volume ratio causes smaller nanoparticles to melt or become disordered at lower temperatures.
The simulated nanoparticles begin in a low-temperature crystalline state with a well-defined atomic arrangement.
A controlled thermal ramp can be applied in atomistic molecular dynamics using an interatomic potential and a thermostat such as Nosé–Hoover.
The proposed simulations are performed on isolated nanoparticles in vacuum.
Nanoparticle size is systematically varied from a few nanometers to tens of nanometers while using a consistent heating rate.
Changing nanoparticle size changes its surface-to-volume ratio.
A higher surface-to-volume ratio enhances surface effects in smaller nanoparticles.
Enhanced surface effects increase atomic mobility.
Increased atomic mobility causes an earlier onset of structural disorder or melting.
The critical temperature for melting or structural disorder increases with nanoparticle size.
The initial low-temperature crystalline state has minimal atomic motion and stable interatomic bonds.
Vacuum molecular dynamics simulations may omit environmental effects such as oxidation and substrate influence.
Radial distribution functions, coordination numbers, and mean-square displacements can be used to identify the onset of melting or structural disorder.
The qualitative size trend is expected, but the quantitative relationship between nanoparticle size and thermal-stability thresholds is uncertain and requires experimental verification.
